```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse=TRUE,comment="#>")
library("coherent4cast")
```

## Evaluate predictions on eligible held-out subjects

The following small numerical example illustrates the metric definitions. It
is not an empirical assessment of predictive performance. Subjects are free of
the terminal event at the assessment origin; `time` is follow-up from that
origin and `status` marks an observed terminal event.

```{r metrics}
risk <- c(.08,.12,.18,.25,.32,.48,.63,.77)
time <- c(5,4,1,6,2,4,1.5,3)
status <- c(0,1,1,0,1,0,1,1)
v <- validate(risk,time,status,horizon=3,threshold=.3)
v$metrics
v$confusion
v$assumptions
```

The Brier score measures squared probability error. AUROC compares a case's
risk with a control's risk, assigning half credit to ties; it does not assess
calibration. Calibration-in-the-large is an intercept with predicted log odds
as an offset. The calibration slope also estimates their multiplier. ICI is
the weighted mean absolute difference between smoothed observed probabilities
and predicted probabilities. Small samples can make a calibration statistic
undefined or unstable; inspect the returned diagnostic.

Inverse probabilities of censoring weight observed cases and horizon controls.
The default Kaplan-Meier estimate requires marginal independent censoring.
History-dependent censoring instead needs justified conditional probabilities:

```{r conditional}
validate(risk,time,status,3,
  censor_survival=list(case=rep(.9,8),horizon=rep(.8,8)))$metrics
```

The vectors above are illustrative supplied probabilities, not estimated
censoring models. The user must justify their conditioning and positivity.
Sensitivity, specificity, predictive values and net benefit use the same
weighted two-by-two table and the explicitly selected decision threshold.

## Construct prediction sets with their sampling assumptions

```{r conformal}
scores <- c(.05,.1,.12,.2,.22,.31,.35,.5,.6,.8)
candidates <- seq(.1,.9,by=.1)
sets <- rc_conformal(scores,candidates,alpha=.2)
sets$candidates
sets$coverage_guarantee
```

Calibration subjects must be separated from training. Known importance weights
require weighted exchangeability. Estimated weights alone do not provide an
exact finite-sample guarantee. A certified calculation accepts externally
justified simultaneous weight intervals and charges their error probability:

```{r certified}
certified <- rc_conformal(scores,candidates,alpha=.2,
   weight_status="certified",weight_lower=rep(.8,10),
   weight_upper=rep(1.2,10),candidate_weight_upper=rep(1.2,9),
   band_error=.02)
certified$candidates
```

These calls invert a supplied candidate grid. They do not automatically recover
an entire continuous outcome set or certify arbitrary temporal drift.

## Keep uncertainty procedures distinct

```{r bands}
b <- rc_band(theta=c(-2,.2),covariance=diag(c(.04,.01)),
   forecast=function(theta)plogis(theta[1]+theta[2]*c(0,1)),
   draws=1000,seed=21)
data.frame(estimate=b$estimate,lower=b$lower,upper=b$upper)
b$method
```

This is frequentist Gaussian resampling through a nonlinear forecast. It is not
a Bayesian posterior or finite-sample confidence projection. `rc_regularize()`
offers observed-information log-determinant stabilization for an eligible
exact-history fit; it does not guarantee automatic Firth bias cancellation.
For independent uncensored terminal times with known frailty dispersion and a
constant baseline, `rc_pivot()` supplies a different, exact model-specific route.
